answers.question: List of scenarios
answer: Orderly – 'Net zero by 2050' scenario (NGFS Orderly / IPCC SSP1-1.9)
Disorderly – 'Delayed Transition' scenario (NGFS Disorderly / IPCC SSP1-2.6)
Too Little, Too Late – 'Fragmented World' scenario (NGFS Fragmented World / IPCC SSP2-4.5)
Hot House World – 'Current Policies' scenario (NGFS Hot House World / IPCC SSP5-8.5)
answers.evidence: "We adopted the following scenario to assess our business strategy: • Orderly – 'Net zero by 2050' scenario, under which the increase in global surface temperatures is limited to ~1.5°C. • Disorderly – 'Delayed Transition' scenario, under which the increase in global surface temperatures is limited to below 2°C; • 'Hot house World – 'Current Policies' scenario, under which global surface temperatures are in exceedance of 3°C." And from Appendix 3: "Transition risks were identified and rated against the backdrop of a NGFS Orderly 'Net zero by 2050' Transition / IPCC AR6 SSP1-1.9y, the NGFS Disorderly 'Delayed Transition' / IPCC AR6 SSSP1-2.6 and NGFS Fragmented World - 'Too little, too late' / IPCC SSP2-4.5 scenarios."
answers.notes: Four distinct scenarios are used: three for transition risk assessment (Orderly, Disorderly, Too Little Too Late) and three for physical risk assessment (Disorderly, Too Little Too Late, Hot House World). The Orderly scenario is used only for transition risk; the Hot House World only for physical risk. The document names them clearly across multiple pages.
answers.ani_notes: ORDERLY SCENARIO; DISORDERLY SCENARIO; HOT HOUSE WORLD

answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer: Four temperature outcomes are described: ~1.4°C (SSP1-1.9 / NGFS Orderly ~1.5°C), ~1.8°C (SSP1-2.6 / NGFS Disorderly ~1.7°C), ~2.7°C (SSP2-4.5 / NGFS Fragmented World ~2.6°C), and ~4.4°C (SSP5-8.5 / NGFS Hot House World ~3°C). The entity-level scenario narratives describe: +1.5°C (Orderly), <+2°C (Disorderly), and >+3°C (Hot House World). Temperature overshoot is mentioned in the context of testing pathways "with and without target overshoot".
answers.evidence: "SSP1-1.9 ~1.4°C; SSP1-2.6 ~1.8°C; SSP2 – 4.5 ~2.7°C; SSP5-8.5 ~4.4°C" and "Orderly – Net Zero ~1.5°C; Disorderly – Delayed Transition ~1.7°C; Fragmented World – Too Little, Too Late ~2.6°C; Hot House World – current policies ~3°C" (Appendix 3). Scenario narratives: "Average global temperature +1.5°C" (Orderly), "Average global temperature <+2°C" (Disorderly), "Average global temperature >+3°C" (Hot House World). Overshoot: "two pathways under which the international community achieves our collective net zero targets, (with and without target overshoot)".
answers.notes: Temperature outcomes are stated both at the IPCC SSP level and the NGFS scenario level in Appendix 3, and also summarised in the scenario narrative pages.

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.evidence: "CIAL adopted global data sets (IPCC and NGFS), and downscaled NIWA data to inform physical risk exposure." And: "To develop the scenarios, a team of subject matter experts from across the business participated in a workshop session, facilitated by Deloitte, and followed the process outlined in the table opposite." And: "we used NIWA's downscaled data for these scenarios to understand the climate change projections for Christchurch and the Canterbury region (Eastern South Island)."
answers.notes: The scenarios are customised in two ways: (1) NIWA downscaled global SSP/RCP data to the Christchurch/Canterbury regional level; (2) CIAL developed entity-level narrative scenarios through internal workshops facilitated by Deloitte, drawing on multiple sector scenario archetypes and adapting them to CIAL's specific aviation context and driving forces.
answers.ani_notes: Yes; To review the scenarios a group of subject matter experts conducted a workshop and considered changes in the domestic, global and sectoral scenario context, including developments in scenario archetypes (including updated NGFS scenarios, NIWA’s downscaled AR6 data) and The Aotearoa Circle’s Transport Sector Climate Change Scenarios (released in June 2024). This workshop resulted in the driving forces and scenarios agreed in FY24 being supplemented with additional information.

answers.question: Time frames
answers.answer: Two sets of time horizons are used: (1) For transition risks: short-term 2025–2029, medium-term 2030–2039, long-term 2040–2054 (30-year horizon total). (2) For physical risks: three strategic points in time — 2030 (short-term: now to 2029), 2050 (medium-term: 2030–2050), and 2100 (long-term: 2050–2100). Rationales are provided for both sets of timeframes.
answers.evidence: "Transition risks were considered over a 30-year time horizon (i.e. a shorter horizon than applied for our physical risk assessment), on the basis that the next 30 years are critical for the transition to a decarbonised economy. The short-term timeframe is current day to 5 years into the future (2025 – 2029), medium-term 5-15 years (2030– 2039), and long-term 15-30 years (2040 – 2054). These time horizons were chosen to align with our strategic planning horizons." And: "Physical risks were considered at three strategic points in time (2030, 2050, and 2100). These time horizons were chosen to align with our strategic planning horizons and asset design life and renewal cycles. This will help to ensure that any major capital infrastructure investments we make in the short-to-medium term incorporate the appropriate design specifications to withstand climate stressors that are projected to be in effect toward the end of the century."
answers.location_hint: Page 10 (Risk Assessment Process) and page 12 (Physical Risks timeframe key)
answers.notes: Rationales are explicitly provided for both sets of timeframes: transition timeframes align with strategic planning horizons and the critical 30-year decarbonisation window; physical risk timeframes align with strategic planning horizons and asset design life/renewal cycles.
answers.ani_notes: Short term: (2025- 2030); Medium term (2030- 2050); Long term (2050-2100)

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.evidence: "CCC pathways and sector scenarios were not used to inform physical and transition risk exposure; given the global drivers that influence the aviation sector, CIAL adopted global data sets (IPCC and NGFS), and downscaled NIWA data to inform physical risk exposure. In this regard, CCC pathways and sector scenarios were referenced in a qualitative context only, to inform the types of national policy settings that would be in place and the way alternative futures might plausibly develop under scenarios." And: "we changed the scenarios used to assess these, replacing the 'Hot House World' scenario with the 'Too Little, Too Late' scenario, on the basis that transition risks do not surface prior to 2050 in the Hot House World scenario."
answers.notes: The document provides explicit justifications for: (1) choosing IPCC/NGFS global datasets over CCC national scenarios (due to global drivers of aviation); (2) using NIWA downscaled data for physical risk (to get Christchurch/Canterbury regional projections); (3) replacing the Hot House World scenario with Too Little Too Late for transition risk assessment (because transition risks don't surface before 2050 in the Hot House World scenario).
answers.ani_notes: Yes; CIAL’s view of the key driving forces was determined, with participants choosing from a long list drawn from various sector scenarios, including New Zealand Green Building Council; Aotearoa Circle’s Tourism sector scenarios; and the Aviation sector’s WayPoint 2050 Technology and SAF/Fuel availability scenarios. In 2025 driving forces identified in Aotearoa Circle’s Transport Sector Scenarios were also considered. The modelling which is inherent in these sector scenario archetypes is the extent of the modelling used by CIAL in its scenario analysis.
